6: Matthew and Luke both give a genealogy, and they do not match. Matthew runs forward from Abraham to Joseph in three groups of fourteen, making a Jewish and royal case; Luke runs backward from Jesus to Adam and on to God, making a universal one. Between David and Joseph the two lists agree on only two names, Shealtiel and Zerubbabel, and even there the fathers named differ. Ancient genealogies routinely served argument rather than registry, and readers have proposed levirate marriage, adoption, or a Marian line for Luke. The honest starting point is to ask what each writer is claiming, not which list is the birth certificate.
7: Matthew tells the infancy from Joseph’s side — his dreams, his decisions, the flight into Egypt. Luke tells it from Mary’s — her visit from Gabriel, her visit to Elisabeth, her song. Neither infancy narrative shows clear literary dependence on the other; whether either author knew the other’s work remains debated. Where they overlap (Bethlehem, Nazareth, the virgin conception, Joseph in David’s line) is worth noting precisely because it is small. On dating: Herod the Great died in 4 BC, so the nativity must fall before that — most commonly placed at 6–4 BC. The census under Quirinius (Luke 2:2) is the hardest datum to reconcile, since Quirinius’ known Syrian governorship and census fall in AD 6; proposals include an earlier term of office, a different sense of "first," or a separate enrollment. No solution commands agreement.
13: Luke dates the beginning of John’s ministry precisely — the fifteenth year of Tiberius (Luke 3:1), which by the usual reckoning is AD 28 or 29 — and anchors it further with Pilate, Herod Antipas, Philip, Lysanias, Annas and Caiaphas. It is the most carefully dated moment in the gospels, and every other date in Jesus’ ministry is calculated outward from it.
24: John counts three Passovers in the ministry (2:13, 6:4, 11:55), which is where the traditional three-year ministry comes from. The synoptics mention only the final Passover and do not provide John’s explicit multi-Passover framework. This is not a contradiction so much as a difference in scope — but it is the reason estimates of the ministry’s length range from one year to three and a half.
25: John places this cleansing at the beginning of Jesus’ ministry, at his first Passover in Jerusalem (John 2:13). The synoptics place a cleansing in the last week of his life (¶273). Some readers take these as two separate acts, others as one act reported at different points in the narrative for different purposes — John opening his gospel with a claim on the temple, the synoptics making it the act that provokes the arrest.
51: The Beatitudes: Matthew gives eight blessings in the third person on a mountain, then turns and addresses the hearers directly in a ninth (5:11). Luke gives four in the second person on a plain, each paired with a woe. Matthew qualifies "poor" with "in spirit" and hunger with "for righteousness"; Luke directly addresses "you poor" and "you who hunger now." Both readings are the text. 3 Nephi 12 follows Matthew’s wording and adds to it.
77: The Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 5–7) and the Sermon on the Plain (Luke 6:20–49) contain much of the same material in the same order, but Matthew’s is roughly three times longer and set on a mountain, Luke’s shorter and set on level ground. Most of Matthew’s extra material appears elsewhere in Luke, scattered through the travel narrative. Whether these are two sermons or one sermon reported twice is a real question, not a settled one.
146: The feeding of the five thousand is the only miracle before the passion that all four gospels tell. That makes it the best available control case: read the four columns here and you can see the characteristic habits of each writer on identical material.
149: John alone follows the feeding with the Bread of Life discourse (John 6:22–71) — the synoptics have no equivalent. John repeatedly converts a sign into a discourse in which Jesus interprets it; the synoptics leave the act to speak.
158: Peter’s confession reads differently in each synoptic: Mark has "Thou art the Christ" (8:29), Luke "The Christ of God" (9:20), Matthew "Thou art the Christ, the Son of the living God" (16:16) followed by the blessing on Peter and the keys — material found in no other gospel. Whatever one concludes about its origin, the difference in what each writer chose to record is on the page.
267: Matthew and Mark put this anointing two days before the Passover (Matt. 26:2; Mark 14:1), John six days before it (John 12:1), and John alone names the woman as Mary of Bethany and the objector as Judas. Luke 7:36–50 tells a similar story in Galilee, much earlier, with a different point entirely. The accounts are printed together here so the differences can be seen — not as a claim that they are one occasion.
269: John dates the triumphal entry the day after the supper at Bethany (12:1, 12:12); the synoptics place the entry first and the anointing later in the week (Matt. 26:6; Mark 14:3). The events are the same; the order is not. Read ¶267 and ¶306 alongside this one.
273: Here the synoptics place the cleansing: in Holy Week, days before the arrest, as the act that hardens official opposition. John reported a cleansing three years earlier (¶25). This column set therefore compares Matthew, Mark and Luke against a John passage held by many readers to describe a different occasion.
306: The anointing at Bethany appears here again, at its place in the passion sequence. On the dating and on the identity of the woman, see the note at ¶267. Luke’s anointing (7:36–50) is almost certainly a separate event and is shown for comparison only.
308: Passover reckoning. In the synoptics the Last Supper is the Passover meal, eaten after sundown beginning 15 Nisan. In John, Jesus dies as the Passover lambs are killed on 14 Nisan, and the meal precedes the feast (John 13:1; 18:28; 19:14). Explanations offered include differing calendars, differing reckonings of when the day begins, and Johannine theological arrangement making Jesus the lamb. No explanation has carried the field.
311: Whether this meal was the Passover itself turns on the same difference of reckoning described at ¶308. Read the synoptic accounts and John 13 side by side and note what each writer chooses to report about the meal — the synoptics the bread and cup, John the washing of feet.
344: The hour of the crucifixion. Mark 15:25 has the third hour; John 19:14 has Pilate still judging about the sixth. Proposed resolutions include Roman versus Jewish hour-counting and approximate three-hour blocks in ordinary ancient speech. The disagreement is in the manuscripts, not in the translation. On the year: the crucifixion is normally placed at AD 30 or AD 33, the two years in which 14 Nisan fell on a Friday during Pilate’s prefecture (AD 26–36). AD 30 fits a ministry begun about AD 28–29; AD 33 fits John’s three Passovers more comfortably.
347: The words from the cross differ by gospel and barely overlap: Mark and Matthew record one (the cry of dereliction), Luke three, John three. Only Luke and John record any saying the other does. Read down the columns and notice that each gospel’s selection matches the portrait it has been building throughout.
352: The resurrection appearances cannot be laid end to end without choices. The women differ by name and number, the angels by count, and the locations diverge — Matthew and Mark point to Galilee, Luke keeps everything in and near Jerusalem, John has both. Paul’s earlier list (1 Corinthians 15:3–8, at ¶361) matches none of them exactly and names appearances no gospel records.
note: Places where the gospels arrange or report the same event differently. Where John’s sequence diverges from the synoptics, or the synoptics diverge among themselves, the pericope states the difference and the usual explanations rather than harmonizing it silently.
